analysis.one_liner: Bars health plans from treating mental health and addiction care worse than physical care.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Republican with 26 cosponsors from both parties, never got a committee vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped health insurance plans from putting tougher copays, visit limits, and annual or lifetime dollar caps on mental health and substance abuse treatment than they put on other medical care. It also would have closed loopholes in the partial mental health parity law passed in 1996, which applied only to dollar caps, let plans off the hook if costs rose more than 1%, and expired. And it would have extended the rule to people buying insurance on their own, not just through an employer. The bill was sent to three House committees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental illness or substance abuse disorders, and their families, would have gotten insurance coverage for treatment on the same terms as coverage for physical illness — equal copays, equal visit limits, and no separate annual or lifetime caps. Mental health and addiction treatment providers would have gained patients who could actually pay for care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing mental health or addiction care

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited group and individual health plans from imposing treatment limits or financial requirements on mental health benefits if similar limits were not imposed on medical and surgical benefits in comparable settings, including inpatient and outpatient care [S3].
It applied the same parity rule to substance abuse and chemical dependency benefits [S3].
It removed the 1996 law's exemption for plans whose costs would rise more than 1% and its sunset date, and it extended parity to coverage sold in the individual market, not just employer plans [S3].
It defined financial requirements broadly to include copayments, deductibles, out-of-network charges, out-of-pocket contributions, and annual and lifetime aggregate limits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who sponsor group health plans and the insurers who administer them would have borne the cost of equalizing benefits, likely passed to all plan members through higher premiums. Insurers would also have faced new compliance requirements, though the bill preserved their ability to manage care through prior authorization and medical necessity review.

drawbacks.text: The bill did not require any plan to offer mental health benefits at all — it only regulated how plans that do offer them must structure the benefits — so a plan could legally drop mental health coverage entirely to escape the rule [S3].

Plans kept their ability to set separate reimbursement rates and to use pre-admission screening, prior authorization, and medical-necessity rules to limit services, so the bill would not have stopped all coverage denials [S3].

Equalizing benefits would have raised premiums for employers and workers, since mental health and addiction treatment that was previously limited or excluded would have been covered on par with medical care — a real cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending a two-tier system that treated mental illness and addiction as less legitimate than physical illness — is real and large for the millions of people affected. The costs were also real: higher premiums spread across everyone with employer coverage. The biggest design weakness is the escape hatch: because plans were never required to offer mental health benefits, the bill's protection could be avoided by dropping the coverage altogether, a loophole Congress did not close here.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then to subcommittees, none of which ever reported it out, and it died when Congress ended in January 1999 without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Marge Roukema, a New Jersey Republican, introduced the bill on March 26, 1998, joined by five original cosponsors from both parties [S1][S3].
The same day, the House referred it to three committees — Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — a split referral that meant it needed attention from all three to move [S5].
In April and May 1998 it was further referred to subcommittees on Health, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations [S5].
The last recorded action was the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 5, 1998; no committee ever marked up or reported the bill [S5].
The bill had 26 cosponsors, 22 Democrats and 4 Republicans, but never received a committee or floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers sponsoring group plans were better off, because they avoided a requirement to equalize mental health and addiction benefits — and people needing that care were left with the 1996 law's weaker, expiring protections.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and 26 members from both parties — 22 Democrats and 4 Republicans — cosponsored it; the record shows no partisan opposition, only inaction.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to equalize copays, visit limits, and annual or lifetime caps across mental health, addiction, and medical care, ending a practice that shifted costs onto people with mental illness. Plans kept their managed-care tools, but the core restriction on their benefit design would have gone.
Employers would have absorbed higher benefit costs, likely passed to workers through premiums, though plans under collective bargaining agreements got a delayed effective date.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance abuse treatment providers
industries.note: Therapists, psychiatric hospitals, and addiction treatment programs would have gained patients able to pay for care, since coverage limits that ration their services would have to match limits on other medicine.
